businessType: Mid/large commercial staffing firm operating a national branch network. Two reportable streams: (1) temporary/contract staffing (~80% of revenue), where the firm earns the spread between client bill rate and worker pay rate; (2) permanent / direct-hire placement (~20% of revenue), a fee-based, demand-leading service. Revenue concentrated in light-industrial, logistics, clerical, and administrative verticals. Internal headcount is mostly recruiters and branch staff carried as a largely fixed cost.
stage: FY2025: Revenue $1,500M (+5.0% YoY vs $1,429M FY2024, decelerating sharply from +12% the prior year). Mix: temp/contract $1,200M (~80%), perm/direct-hire $300M (~20%). Permanent placement revenue DOWN -8% YoY. Gross margin (blended bill-pay spread plus perm fees) 19.5%, down from 21.0% prior year. SG&A ~13.5% of revenue (recruiters, branches), roughly fixed and grew with the prior expansion. EBITDA $90M (6.0% margin) vs $114.3M (8.0%) prior year, a 200 bps decline. Internal staff headcount +4% YoY (added ahead of demand). Client orders -6% YoY; temp hours per week trending -2% sequentially in recent quarters.
ownerGoal: Decide before the next quarter (~90 days) whether to freeze internal hiring and right-size the branch/recruiter footprint ahead of a possible demand downturn, or to hold capacity to capture a rebound. Protect EBITDA margin and return to profitable growth without either (a) being caught with excess fixed capacity into a softening cycle or (b) gutting the recruiter base needed to capture a recovery.
ownerConstraints: Bill-rate constraint: bill rates are capped by client budgets and intense competition for orders; clients are resisting the bill-rate increases needed to fully pass through wage inflation, so the firm cannot simply re-price the temp book at will.

Capacity / rebound constraint: recruiter and branch capacity cannot be cut too fast — recruiter tenure and client relationships take 6-12 months to rebuild, so over-cutting destroys the ability to capture a demand rebound.
Cost-input constraint: worker wage inflation is running ~6% and is largely outside the firm's control; pay rates must stay competitive to fill orders, which compresses the spread when bill rates lag.
Fixed-commitment constraint: branch lease commitments are multi-year; the firm cannot instantly shed branch occupancy cost even where order volume has fallen.

Client-concentration constraint: a meaningful share of temp hours sits with a small number of large light-industrial/logistics clients whose order volumes are the most economically sensitive, so demand softening is concentrated and lumpy.
Workforce constraint: temp workers are contingent and re-deployable, but losing skilled recruiters during a freeze risks permanent loss of fill capability in key verticals.
immediateConcern: EBITDA margin fell 200 bps in one year (8.0% to 6.0%) while revenue still grew 5%. Leadership cannot tell how much of the decline is a controllable spread/pricing problem versus a softening demand cycle that the cost base has not adjusted to. Permanent placement (the leading indicator) is already down -8%, client orders are down -6%, and internal staff grew +4% — yet the firm keeps adding capacity against a forecast that may be rolling over. The CEO must commit a capacity decision within 90 days and a wrong call in either direction is costly.
